questions.question: Why do teams adopt LangChain in production LLM apps?
options: To avoid writing any tests.
To replace HTTP APIs entirely.
To run LLMs faster by caching all responses.
To compose models, tools, retrieval, and parsing with reusable interfaces.
questions.explanation: LangChain provides standardized building blocks — chains, retrievers, tools, parsers — so teams can wire together LLM workflows without reimplementing integration plumbing for every new component.

questions.question: When is a deterministic chain usually better than an agent?
options: When there are many unknown tool choices at runtime.
When you need human-in-the-loop pauses.
When workflow steps are fixed and predictable.
When every request must branch differently.
questions.explanation: A deterministic chain follows a fixed sequence that is easy to test and trace; agents introduce dynamic tool selection which adds unpredictability and debugging cost that is only justified when the workflow is genuinely open-ended.

questions.question: What is a primary purpose of tools in LangChain?
options: Allow model-driven calls to external capabilities.
Convert SQL to Python syntax.
Replace retrieval systems.
Store vector embeddings automatically.
questions.explanation: Tools give the model a way to call external capabilities like search engines, APIs, or databases; without tools the model can only generate text from its training data.

questions.question: Which issue most directly causes weak RAG answers?
options: Using structured output instead of plain text.
Retrieving irrelevant or stale context chunks.
Chunking documents into pieces that are too large.
Calling the LLM API more than once per request.
questions.explanation: RAG quality is bounded by retrieval quality — if the retrieved chunks are irrelevant or outdated, even a capable model cannot produce a correct answer from bad context.

questions.question: Why is structured output important?
options: It yields predictable machine-usable fields instead of brittle text parsing.
It eliminates all model errors.
It removes the need for validation.
It works only with one provider.
questions.explanation: Structured outputs return typed fields that downstream code can access reliably; free-text responses require fragile string parsing that breaks whenever the model changes its phrasing.

questions.question: What should observability logs include for debugging LLM workflows?
options: Only final answers.
Only latency numbers.
Prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, outputs, and errors.
Only model name and temperature.
questions.explanation: End-to-end tracing across prompts, retrieved chunks, tool invocations, and model outputs is necessary to locate where a workflow produces wrong results — latency alone tells you nothing about correctness.

questions.question: What is a common safety practice for tool-enabled agents?
options: Skip input schemas for faster execution.
Grant full write access by default.
Disable error handling to expose raw traces.
Limit tool scope and enforce permission policies.
questions.explanation: Restricting what tools can read or write limits damage when the model makes an incorrect decision; granting broad access by default amplifies every model mistake into a potentially destructive action.

questions.question: How should provider changes be handled in a LangChain app?
options: Remove retrieval before migrating providers.
Use shared interfaces and evaluate behavior changes with tests and traces.
Hardcode one provider forever.
Switch providers without retesting.
questions.explanation: Shared interfaces isolate the provider swap to one configuration point, but models from different providers behave differently; you must re-evaluate outputs with tests and traces rather than assuming drop-in compatibility.
